questions.statement: It was the heavy traffic ____ delayed the school bus yesterday.
questions.context: A parent asks why a school transport arrived late on a weekday.

options.feedback: Correct! 'It was ... that' is the standard cleft pattern and it focuses the heavy traffic.
'Which' can be used in a cleft about a person, but the subject here is a situation, not a person.
'What' introduces a relative clause about a thing, not the focus of a cleft sentence.
'Who' refers to people and cannot link to the heavy traffic.

questions.explanation:
The cleft 'It was ... that' keeps the auxiliary in 'was' and isolates the element that answers the question.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It was on the bus ____ I first heard about the exchange programme.
questions.context: A student recalls when a piece of news reached him during a journey.

options.feedback: 'When' introduces a time clause and would need a time expression rather than a place.
Correct! 'It was on the bus that' is the standard cleft and it focuses the place of the event.
'Where' introduces a relative clause about a place and does not build a cleft.
'Which' cannot be used as the relative pronoun of a cleft in this structure.

questions.explanation:
Cleft sentences move one element to the front and add 'it', so the reader is told exactly what the sentence is about.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What I need ____ a quiet place to study.
questions.context: A student explains what a good study place provides.

options.feedback: 'Are' would not agree with the singular subject 'what I need'.
'Were' is the past and the need is present.
Correct! 'What I need is' is the wh-cleft pattern and it focuses the complement.
'Was' is the past simple, which the present need does not allow.

questions.explanation:
The wh-cleft keeps a complete clause after the question word and then states the missing information as the complement.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It was my brother ____ helped me with the mathematics homework.
questions.context: A student acknowledges the help a relative gave with school work.

options.feedback: 'Which' is used for things in this pattern, and the focus is a person.
'That' is possible in a cleft about a thing but reads oddly with a personal subject here.
'What' introduces a clause that is the subject, which is a different construction.
Correct! 'It was ... who' is a cleft about a person, and 'who' is the natural relative pronoun here.

questions.explanation:
Cleft sentences about people use 'who' and about things use 'that', which is the pair the question tests.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The place I wanted to visit ____ the coastal town we passed yesterday.
questions.context: A traveller describes a place seen during a road journey.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Was' is the verb of the main clause and agrees with the singular subject 'the place'.
'Were' would not agree with a singular subject.
'Is' is the present, and the reference to a place passed yesterday is a past event.
'Are' would not agree with 'the place' in any tense.

questions.explanation:
A cleft can be built without 'it': a relative clause first, then the main clause, and the information lands at the end.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It is not the money ____ he lacks; it is the time.
questions.context: A person explains the real obstacle in a personal project.

options.feedback: 'He' cannot serve as the relative pronoun in this structure.
Correct! The negative cleft 'It is not the money that he lacks' focuses the true contrast.
'Which' refers to things but the cleft with a person subject is normally built with 'that' or 'who'.
'Who' refers to people, and the clause is about the person, not the pronoun.

questions.explanation:
A negative cleft denies the expected element and then gives the real one, which sharpens the contrast in the second clause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The reason the class was late ____ the storm blocked the road.
questions.context: A teacher explains a delay to the students at the start of a lesson.

options.feedback: 'Were' would not agree with the singular subject 'the reason'.
'Has been' would place the explanation before the present moment.
Correct! 'Was' links the subject 'the reason' with the explanation in the second clause.
'Will be' would predict a future explanation.

questions.explanation:
A cleft beginning with 'the reason' states the cause last, which puts emphasis on the explanation itself.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It was not until the lights went out ____ the students realised how late it was.
questions.context: A class describes the moment it became aware of the hour of the evening.

options.feedback: 'When' would introduce a time clause but not this cleft pattern.
'Which' cannot be the relative pronoun of a cleft about a limit in time.
'Then' is an adverb of sequence and cannot serve as a relative pronoun.
Correct! 'It was not until ... that' is the standard cleft for a limit in time.

questions.explanation:
The 'not until' cleft stresses a moment and is very common in speech when a late realisation is reported.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This is the house ____ I spent my childhood.
questions.context: An adult points out a building that plays a part in a family history.

options.feedback: Correct! 'That' is the relative pronoun of a cleft about a place when the following clause carries a verb and no preposition.
'Where' would require a clause without a verb such as 'where I lived'.
'Which' would be used in a cleft about a thing but not about a person and a place together.
'What' introduces a subject clause, not a cleft after 'the house'.

questions.explanation:
After a clefted noun with a possessive relative clause, 'that' is preferred over a prepositional 'where', which would need a different verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The thing I want to complain about ____ the noise from the construction site.
questions.context: A resident explains a complaint to a neighbour near a building site.

options.feedback: 'Are' would not agree with a singular subject.
Correct! 'Is' links the subject 'the thing' with the complaint in the present.
'Was' is the past, and the complaint is current.
'Were' would not agree with the singular subject in any case.

questions.explanation:
This cleft puts a relative clause first so that the complaint itself receives the emphasis at the end of the sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It ____ my grandmother who taught me to cook.
questions.context: A speaker credits a relative for a domestic skill learned in childhood.

options.feedback: 'Is' is the present, and the teaching belongs to the past.
'Were' would not agree with 'it'.
Correct! 'It was' is the auxiliary of the cleft and agrees with the singular subject 'it'.
'Has been' would place the action in a period that is not over.

questions.explanation:
In this cleft the relative clause is the longest element and the shortest one, the name, comes after 'was'.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When I lost my keys ____ it was my brother who found them under the mat.
questions.context: A person answers a question about the end of a frustrating search.

options.feedback: 'Was' alone has no subject in front of it, so the clause is incomplete.
'There was' would introduce existence, and the sentence states a fact, not the existence of an event.
'He was' would duplicate the subject already given in the relative clause.
Correct! 'It was' introduces the cleft and lets the emphasis fall on the person who found the keys.

questions.explanation:
Embedding a cleft after a 'when' clause requires the dummy subject 'it' again, because the sentence has to remain grammatical on its own.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It is the delay of the results ____ worries the students most.
questions.context: A class reacts to a long wait for the publication of a grade list.

options.feedback: Correct! 'That' links the clefted subject to the verb 'worries' in a cleft about a thing.
'Which' is possible in a cleft about a person, and here the focus is a delay.
'What' introduces a clause acting as the subject, which is a different structure.
'Who' refers to people, and a delay is not a person.

questions.explanation:
When the clefted element is the subject of the relative clause, the pronoun is normally 'that'.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The person who organised the event ____ the head of the sports department.
questions.context: A school announces who was responsible for a school activity.

options.feedback: 'Were' would not agree with the singular subject 'the person'.
Correct! 'Was' is the verb of the main clause, in past simple to match the relative clause.
'Has been' would suggest the role is still held and the event is recent.
'Will be' would place the identification in the future.

questions.explanation:
A cleft formed with a relative clause in front states the answer at the end, which is where the emphasis belongs.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It was the lack of practice ____ made the performance so nervous.
questions.context: A teacher analyses why a student was nervous on stage.

options.feedback: 'Which' is not used for a clefted subject in this pattern.
'What' introduces a clause serving as the subject of the main verb, not a cleft.
Correct! 'That' completes the cleft and links the cause to the result described after it.
'Who' refers to people, and a lack of practice is an abstract thing.

questions.explanation:
A cleft with 'it' keeps the rest of the sentence intact and simply adds the focus on one element.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What surprised me most ____ the sudden change in the weather.
questions.context: A traveller describes an unexpected experience during a trip.

options.feedback: 'Were' would not agree with a singular subject.
'Is' is the present, and the surprise belongs to a past moment.
'Are' would not agree with the subject and would be plural.
Correct! 'Was' agrees with the singular subject 'what surprised me most'.

questions.explanation:
The wh-cleft is built with a complete clause after the question word, and the verb then agrees with that whole clause treated as the subject.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It is in the school library ____ the study group meets every afternoon.
questions.context: A student tells a visitor where an extracurricular group gathers.

options.feedback: Correct! 'It is ... that' is the standard cleft for a place with a full relative clause after it.
'Where' would be used in a cleft with a clause that has no verb of its own, such as 'where the group sits'.
'Which' cannot be the relative pronoun of this cleft about a place.
'When' introduces a time clause, and the clause is about a location.

questions.explanation:
Because the following clause already has a subject and a verb, the cleft needs 'that' rather than a locative relative pronoun.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The only thing that still needs explaining ____ the cause of the error in the budget.
questions.context: An administrator lists the points still pending in a financial review.

options.feedback: 'Are' would not agree with the singular subject 'the only thing'.
Correct! 'Is' links the long subject with the explanation that closes the sentence.
'Were' is the past, and the question is still open.
'Has' would need a complement such as 'been explained' and cannot stand alone.

questions.explanation:
A cleft that starts with a long subject places the new information at the end, which is the whole rhetorical effect.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It was a lack of planning ____ the whole event collapsed.
questions.context: A committee reports the reason an event had to be cancelled.

options.feedback: 'Which' is not the pronoun used for a clefted subject in this pattern.
'What' would make the relative clause the subject of the main verb instead.
Correct! 'That' links the clefted subject to the verb 'collapsed' in the main clause.
'Who' refers to people, and a lack of planning is not a person.

questions.explanation:
The 'it was ... that' cleft is the standard way of blaming one element and giving it the emphasis of the sentence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It was after the meeting ____ the students understood the new schedule.
questions.context: A group reflects on when a decision communicated to them became clear.

options.feedback: 'When' would introduce a time clause but not a cleft, and the sentence as written has no 'when'.
'Which' cannot be the relative pronoun of a cleft about a moment in time.
'Where' introduces a clause about a place.
Correct! 'It was ... that' is the cleft and it focuses the moment when understanding happened.

questions.explanation:
Time is one of the elements most often clefted, because the question is normally about the moment rather than the event.
---
questions.subject: ingles
